before.overview: Mount Cameron is a broad, triple-summited interior Olympic peak (West, Middle, and East tops) in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, about 21 miles southwest of Sequim. It sits at the head of Cameron Basin/Cameron Pass, between the Grand Valley/Grand Pass drainage to the north and the Dosewallips River canyon to the south, and is named for Amos Benson Cameron, an 1890s homesteader who cut the original trail into the basin. There is no short approach: parties typically reach it either from Obstruction Point via Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail (the shorter, more common option), or up the Dosewallips valley from the south (much longer since a 2002 road washout closed vehicle access). Small remnant snowfields (the Cameron Glaciers) cling to the north side of the mountain well into summer.
before.beta: Mount Cameron is a remote, triple-summited peak well off any maintained trail. The standard way up is a long, mostly-easy ridge scramble gained from Cameron Pass via the Grand Pass/Badger Valley trail system out of Obstruction Point (or, on a longer approach, via Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail). From the pass, climbers leave the trail and follow the broad ridge, crossing numerous false summits on mostly Class 1-2 terrain to the true summit; the Class 3-4 spots come only for parties who continue the traverse along the crest to Cameron's other tops. Remnant patches of the Cameron Glaciers and old snow can linger on the ridge's north side into mid-summer.

before.best_season: Late July through September (snow typically lingers on Cameron Pass and Mount Cameron's north-facing slopes into late July; the Obstruction Point access road itself usually doesn't open until early-to-mid July)
before.approach: Primary approach: drive the narrow, one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road (Olympic NP's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft; usually open only early/mid-July through mid-October) 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass, then continue on the Cameron Pass Trail about 3.5 more miles, climbing to Cameron Pass (~6,450-6,500 ft) and the camp sites in the basin below it (roughly 9-10 miles one-way to a base camp, off-trail beyond that to the summit ridge). Alternative southern approach: from Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking, some 8.5 miles from US-101, forcing a long walk/bike up the old roadbed before even reaching the Dosewallips River Trail proper and then the multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin — this route adds many extra miles and is rarely used as the primary option today. From Cameron Pass it is about 1.5 miles east along the ridge, with the scrambling mostly in the last half mile (mid July).
before.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line back down to the Cameron Basin/Cameron Pass camp, then retrace the Cameron Pass Trail and Grand Pass Trail back to the Obstruction Point trailhead (or continue the much longer exit down the Dosewallips if that was the approach used). No rope work or rappels are typical on the standard scramble; the main descent hazards are loose scree/talus on the upper slopes and, early in the season, glissading or downclimbing residual snowfields on north-facing terrain. Dropping straight off the ridge toward Lost Peak in September ran into cliff bands and fourth-class ground; go back along the ridge instead.
before.bail: There is no quick bail option — the nearest reliable exit is back the way you came via Grand Pass to Obstruction Point. Bailing toward the Dosewallips side is a much longer, harder exit because of the 2002 road washout that closed vehicle access several miles from the trailhead.

access.fees: Park entrance: $30 per private vehicle (7 consecutive days) or $55 Olympic NP annual pass. Overnight Wilderness Camping Permit (required for any approach, since this is inherently a multi-day trip): $6 reservation fee plus $8 per person per night, booked through Recreation.gov; no cash accepted in the park.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: No pets on the Grand Valley/Grand Pass/Cameron Pass trails. Bury human waste 6-8 inches deep and at least 200 ft from water; group size limited to 12.
access.permit: Wilderness/backcountry camping permit required for any overnight stay supporting the climb (day climbs need none). Reserved online via Recreation.gov — paper self-registration at trailheads has been discontinued.
access.closures: Obstruction Point Road (the main approach road) is snow-gated in winter/spring, typically opening early-to-mid July and closing again by mid-October — check the NPS Current Road Conditions page before driving. The Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since a January 2002 washout, which sits about a mile beyond the road-end parking some 8.5 miles from US-101, adding about 6.5 miles of road-walking or biking each way to that southern approach.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate, but Mount Cameron sits on the northeastern, rain-shadowed side of the Olympics, so it is markedly drier than the park's famous west-side rainforests (Sequim averages roughly 16-20 in/yr of precipitation versus 140+ in/yr at the Hoh). Snow lingers on Cameron Pass and the peak's north-facing slopes into late July, and afternoon thunderstorms are possible on exposed ridges in August.

bySeason.fall: September often brings the most stable weather and fewest bugs, but the first snow can arrive by early-to-mid October, and Obstruction Point Road closes by mid-October.
bySeason.spring: Obstruction Point Road and the Cameron Pass Trail are typically still snow-covered/closed to vehicle access; not a realistic climbing window.
bySeason.summer: Late July through August is the most reliable snow-free window; Obstruction Point Road usually opens by early-to-mid July.
bySeason.winter: Obstruction Point Road is gated by snow; reaching Cameron requires extended ski/snowshoe mountaineering and is a much more serious undertaking.

approach_variants.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
approach_variants.notes: Read the name on this route with care — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies west of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is Cameron Pass and the test is the direction you turn out of it: the ridge you climb rises to the east. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you. Second test, and it is the one that matters most here: the ridge is a sequence of false summits. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going: the true top is still easy Class 1-2 ground, and steps of Class 3-4 mean you have passed it and are on the traverse. Third test, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route. Carry a map and count your summits.

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect

approach_variants.whyThisWay: When Obstruction Point Road is still closed; longer, with little-maintained tread and heavy brush, but it joins the same route at Cameron Pass.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical once you are at Cameron Pass: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground all the way to the top. The pass is west of the summit whatever the route title says. The extra test this side needs is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them. What going too far looks like: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

approach_variants.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.

approach_variants.whyThisWay: Rarely used now; mostly for parties already on a Dosewallips valley trip, since the closed road adds many miles over either northern approach.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical at the pass: the ridge rises east out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground to the true top. The test this side needs is about which valley you are in, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the route's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first.

expect.beta: The West Peak route starts from the East Peak via the Southeast Glacier approach. The traverse between summits is a wild and fun scramble with decent exposure and more technical difficulty than the East Peak ascent. Three distinct towers require climbing up and over; rock quality on this connecting ridge is notoriously poor — climbers describe it as 'shockingly mobile' loose talus and standard chossy 4th class, not sound rock. The route involves low Class 5 rock climbing up to 5.4, though many climbers solo the final sections. A 50-60 meter rope is recommended for rappelling 4th and 5th class terrain.
expect.descent_text: Most parties reverse the route: from West Peak, cross back over the connecting ridge toward East Fury and descend via the Fury-Luna traverse and Access Col to Access Creek and the Big Beaver Trail. Off the West Peak summit itself, descend by dropping slightly east of the true summit down a chute, then make a descending 'choss-traverse' back west to regain the ridge crest, followed by dirty, ledge-y 4th-class terrain down to a small glacier on the northwest side of the peak, which is then downclimbed or crossed to rejoin the Luna Col traverse back toward Access Creek. A 50-60m rope is recommended and gets used for occasional single-rope-length rappels over 4th-class/low-5th-class steps both on this direct descent and along the East-West Fury connecting ridge if that's the return line - realistically a handful of short raps (estimate 2-4) rather than a fixed rappel sequence. Anchors are natural (horns, slings around blocks or small gendarmes) and not fixed/bolted - this terrain sees very light traffic and carries no in-place gear, so carry cord/slings to build and abandon anchors. Expect loose, chossy rock throughout the descent, especially on the gendarmes and ledge systems, and be prepared for route-finding uncertainty in marginal visibility. Note: the original 1981 solo first ascent of the full connecting West Ridge (a much longer multi-day traverse over several gendarmes, not a standalone summit-day descent) used twelve rappels across four days - that figure describes the entire ridge project, not what a typical party rappels descending from West Peak alone.

set.face: West side: the glacier west of the peak, then steep chimneys to the west ridge
set.beta: The original line to West Fury. Cross the glacier on the west side of the peak, pass the bergschrund, and climb one of two steep, shallow chimneys onto the west ridge; broken ledges and rotten rock lead to a final easy scramble to the summit. No modern grade is recorded; expect steep, loose low-fifth-class rock in the chimneys. The ridge from East Fury is a separate climb.

before.overview: The line of the 1958 first ascent of West Fury, climbed from the west rather than along the ridge from East Fury. From a camp on the upper Challenger Glacier, the party crossed steep heather and cliffs down to the glacier west of Mount Fury. They then climbed two steep, shallow chimneys on loose rock, working around a chockstone, to gain the west ridge, and a short easy scramble led to the summit. The route is remote and committing, and the first party came down in the dark, rappelling and bivouacking.
before.beta: The West Peak route starts from the East Peak via the Southeast Glacier approach. before.turnaround: Given a 12-16+ hour round trip from East Fury with real potential for a forced bivouac, set a firm turnaround time from the East-West Fury saddle to avoid being caught on the loose ridge after dark or in deteriorating weather.
before.rappels: One or two occasional single-rope rappels over 4th- and low-5th-class steps on the ridge; carry a 50-60 m rope
before.face: Connecting ridge crest between East Fury and West Fury summits
before.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
before.comms: Cell phone reception is unreliable or nonexistent in the North Cascades backcountry at Mount Fury's elevation. Satellite messengers (Garmin InReach or similar) are strongly recommended for this remote location. No fixed communication infrastructure exists. Emergency situations require hiking out to Big Beaver area or signaling to park rangers.
before.descent: Reverse the ridge traverse back over the three towers to East Fury, then descend East Fury's east-side glacier/scree gully back to Luna Col; short single-rope-length rappels off the towers are sometimes used. Parties continuing a full Northern Pickets traverse instead carry on northwest along the crest over Swiss, Spectre, Phantom and Crooked Thumb toward Challenger, rather than backtracking east to Luna Col.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: SR 20 milepost 134 parking lot; no parking pass is needed. Descend the Ross Dam Trail toward the lake to reach Ross Lake Resort and arrange a paid water-taxi pickup.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 to the parking lot at milepost 134, roughly 28 miles east of Marblemount. No parking pass is needed to leave a car here.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Landing (water-taxi drop)
waypoints.note: Ross Lake Resort's boat drops climbers here to skip miles of lakeshore trail; self-issue wilderness permit kiosk and start of the Big Beaver Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: Walk down the Ross Dam Trail toward the lake and arrange a paid water-taxi pickup with Ross Lake Resort; the boat runs seasonally, costs about $35 one way, and drops climbers at Big Beaver Landing. Parties who cannot get a boat hike roughly 6 miles of lakeshore trail up the west side of Ross Lake instead.

waypoints.name: Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp on the maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail through old-growth forest, roughly 8 trail miles above Big Beaver Landing.
waypoints.directions: Self-issue a wilderness permit at the kiosk, then follow the maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail up-valley through old-growth cedar. It is about 8 to 10 trail miles of easy walking, passing the Big Beaver backcountry camp, to reach Luna Camp.

waypoints.name: Access Creek crossing
waypoints.note: About 1.5 miles past Luna Camp, leave the maintained trail and ford Big Beaver Creek to pick up the faint, cairned Access Creek climbers' path.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the maintained trail about another 1.5 miles past Luna Camp, then leave it and ford Big Beaver Creek to pick up the faint, cairned climbers' path up Access Creek. This is the single easiest place on the trip to go wrong: in poor visibility parties have committed to the wrong drainage, so find the cairns marking the correct crossing before you commit.

waypoints.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' path up the north flank crosses to the creek's south bank near 3,700 ft where brush thickens, then continues to good camping at the basin below the Luna-McMillan col.
waypoints.directions: Climb steep, pathless forest and heather along the north flank of Access Creek. The cairned path crosses to the south bank near 3,700 ft where the brush thickens, then continues to break out of the timber into the open, meadow-floored basin below Luna Peak, which is far less brushy than the drainages either side of it. Reports call it a few hours of reasonable but sustained hiking.

waypoints.name: Luna Col
waypoints.note: Notch between Luna Peak and a small tower on the Luna-McMillan arm; a small snowfield at the saddle usually provides running water and there's a good camp spot here or ~150 ft below on the east side.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-basin past the camping area at the headwaters, then climb a steep gully and heather system to the notch near 6,100 ft that first opens the view north into Luna Cirque. From there a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass, with one short genuinely steep section and cliff-band route-finding, before gaining the connecting ridge to the col. A small snowfield on the saddle usually gives running water.

waypoints.name: East Fury (ridge traverse start)
waypoints.note: Higher of Fury's twin summits and the start of the ~5.4 YDS, Grade III ridge traverse over three towers to West Fury; loose, exposed rock — rope up for the gendarmes.
waypoints.directions: Leave the col early on a light rack. Cross over Point 7360 and drop a red ledge system to a low-fifth-class crux tower, then climb the East Fury Glacier and arete to the summit. Most parties reach it around four to five hours out of camp.

waypoints.name: West Fury (Mount Fury, West Peak)
waypoints.note: True, officially-named summit of Mount Fury. Descend by reversing the ridge traverse to East Fury, then drop East Fury's east-side glacier/scree gully back to Luna Col.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ridge over three loose towers, with short downclimbs and rappels connecting them. It is roughly 5.4 at its hardest, wildly exposed, and the rock is notoriously mobile choss rather than anything solid, so rope up for the gendarmes and expect two to three hours. Anchors are natural horns and slings you leave behind.

before.detailed_rack: A light rack (a few cams/nuts) for protecting low-5th-class steps and any short raps off the towers; a single 50-60m rope, not doubles; 2-3 pickets or ice screws for glacier travel.
what_to_bring: crampons — East Mount Fury Glacier and residual snow fingers
pro_tips: Leave overnight packs at the East-West Fury saddle before the final push to West Fury to save weight and time on the traverse.
If continuing a full Pickets traverse over Outrigger Peak, stay on its west side rather than topping out to keep the crossing closer to 3rd class instead of low 5th.
Water is scarce along the summit ridge beyond Luna Col — carry more than you think you'll need.
Fewer than roughly 20 parties are believed to have stood on West Fury's true summit as of the mid-2010s — expect no beaten path and minimal fixed protection.
watch_out: Rock on the ridge and its towers is notoriously loose — test every hold and avoid standing below partners.
Weather can turn quickly with no fast retreat available from the exposed connecting ridge.
This is one of the most remote objectives in the Lower 48 — a satellite communicator and a filed trip plan with a hard return date are essential.
before.pro_needs: Protection needs are moderate for the Class 5 pitches; the rock is loose and takes gear poorly, so expect to build anchors from natural horns and slung blocks. Pitons are primarily useful for backup anchors on sketchy sections, though modern climbers typically use cams and nuts. The low angle and moderate protection requirements mean self-rescue capability is more critical than full pro redundancy; if ground-up climbing is necessary, climbers must have experience with trad anchors in granite.
before.approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead (SR 20, milepost 134, ~28 miles east of Marblemount), reaching the Northern Pickets and the base of West Fury's ridge is itself a multi-day approach, not a day hike. The standard option follows the Big Beaver Trail: hike (or take the seasonal Ross Lake Resort water taxi, ~$35 one-way, to Big Beaver Landing) roughly 6 miles up the west shore of Ross Lake to the Big Beaver Creek trailhead, then continue on the maintained Big Beaver Trail up-valley through old-growth cedar past the Big Beaver and Luna backcountry camps to a point about 1.5 miles north of Luna Camp (roughly 10-11 trail miles in). Here you leave the trail, ford Big Beaver Creek, and climb steep, pathless forest and heather along the north side of Access Creek - parties describe a few hours of reasonable hiking - to break out of timber into the open, meadow-floored Access Creek basin below Luna Peak, which is relatively brush-free compared to neighboring drainages. Continue up-basin past a scenic camping area near the Access Creek headwaters, then climb a steep gully/heather system to a notch around 6,100 ft (Access Col) that gives the first view north into Luna Cirque and the Southern Pickets skyline; total distance from the trailhead to a camp near this col is roughly 17 miles with substantial gain, typically a full day or more of travel. From the col, a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus (mostly moderate, with one short, genuinely steep section) works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass/Luna Cirque, then gains the Fury-Luna connecting ridge to reach the base of West Fury's west ridge/northwest side. A second, longer approach option comes in via Whatcom Pass on the Little Beaver Trail (about 18 miles, water taxi recommended) and over Easy Ridge/Perfect Pass, traversing the crest past Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger before dropping into Luna Cirque from the north - this is the line typically used by parties doing a full Pickets traverse rather than a dedicated Fury trip. Water is abundant along Big Beaver and Access Creeks but scarce above Access Col. Hazards: poor visibility has caused parties to pick the wrong drainage off the Big Beaver Trail (some parties cairn the correct creek crossing), loose talus, and cliff-band route-finding while sidehilling into Luna Cirque; gullies dropping into Access Creek involve cliffy downclimbing and occasionally short rappels.
before.descent_text: Most parties reverse the route: from West Peak, cross back over the connecting ridge toward East Fury and descend via the Fury-Luna traverse and Access Col to Access Creek and the Big Beaver Trail. Off the West Peak summit itself, descend by dropping slightly east of the true summit down a chute, then make a descending 'choss-traverse' back west to regain the ridge crest, followed by dirty, ledge-y 4th-class terrain down to a small glacier on the northwest side of the peak, which is then downclimbed or crossed to rejoin the Luna Col traverse back toward Access Creek. A 50-60m rope is recommended and gets used for occasional single-rope-length rappels over 4th-class/low-5th-class steps both on this direct descent and along the East-West Fury connecting ridge if that's the return line - realistically a handful of short raps (estimate 2-4) rather than a fixed rappel sequence. Anchors are natural (horns, slings around blocks or small gendarmes) and not fixed/bolted - this terrain sees very light traffic and carries no in-place gear, so carry cord/slings to build and abandon anchors. Expect loose, chossy rock throughout the descent, especially on the gendarmes and ledge systems, and be prepared for route-finding uncertainty in marginal visibility. Note: the original 1981 solo first ascent of the full connecting West Ridge (a much longer multi-day traverse over several gendarmes, not a standalone summit-day descent) used twelve rappels across four days - that figure describes the entire ridge project, not what a typical party rappels descending from West Peak alone.
before.bail: Retreat by reversing the ridge back to East Fury and down its east-side scree/glacier gully to Luna Col; once past the first tower on the traverse, retreat is slow over extremely loose rock, so many parties treat the push to West Fury as a near-committing outing once underway.

pitch_detail.notes: Hannegan Pass Trail to Whatcom Pass (~18 mi one-way per the original account), then across the crevassed Whatcom Icefall to the cliffs above the Challenger Glacier, descending to a Perfect Pass base camp.
Two steep, loose, 'unpromising' shallow chimneys directly beneath and about 1,000 ft below the west summit; the first-ascent party split to scout alternate lines.
Short, easy scramble from the top of the chimneys to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: An NPS wilderness permit (the Luna cross-country zone is walk-up only, issued in person at Marblemount) and a Ross Lake water taxi reservation are both required and often the limiting factor for scheduling this trip; best conditions are typically mid-July through August.

days.note: Take the Ross Lake water taxi from Ross Dam to Big Beaver Landing to cut several miles of road-walk, then follow the Big Beaver Trail roughly 9-10 miles to Luna Camp. Leave the trail there, bushwhack across Big Beaver Creek and up the notorious Access Creek drainage (devil's club, slide alder, then scree/heather), and climb a steep snow/scree gully to the ridge crest and Luna Col. This is a long, grueling day even before any climbing begins.
days.title: Water taxi + approach to Luna Col
days.objective: Reach high camp at Luna Col (~7,200 ft)

days.note: From Luna Col, cross over Point 7360 and down a red ledge system to a low-5th-class crux tower, then up the East Mount Fury Glacier/arete to East Fury's summit. Continue the exposed ridge traverse over three towers (short rappels/downclimbs between them) to reach West Fury's summit, then reverse the entire traverse back to camp. Most parties treat this as a full 12-16+ hour day and it is the technical and physical crux of the trip.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee for advance permits (current NPS fee structure); North Cascades National Park itself has no entrance fee. Ross Lake Resort's water taxi runs roughly $35-105 per boatload depending on distance and party size (2026 rates).
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Bear canisters are required in some Picket Range camping zones and can be borrowed in person at the Wilderness Information Center (Marblemount) or the Glacier Public Service Center.
access.permit: A backcountry/wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays. Reserve in advance via Recreation.gov (about 60% of backcountry zones/sites are reservable, must be claimed within 3 days of the trip via email to the Wilderness Information Center) or pick up a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (about 40% of sites held for walk-ups). Trail camps such as Luna Camp can be reserved, but the Luna cross-country zone used for the high camp at Luna Col is walk-up only.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes seasonally near the Ross Dam Trailhead, typically from early December to April/May depending on snow and avalanche conditions; check WSDOT's pass report before driving in. Luna Fire closure (as of mid-September 2026): the Big Beaver Trail is closed from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, and Luna Camp, Beaver Pass Camp (with its stock and group camps) and 39 Mile Camp (with 39 Mile Stock) are closed; cross-country zone access from closed trails is prohibited. The closure moves - check current park fire closures before a trip. The alternative Whatcom Pass approach is also affected: the Little Beaver Trail is closed from Little Beaver Camp to the Big Beaver junction, along with the Little Beaver boat-in camp and Perry Creek, under the park's separate long-term closure.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (National Park Service) — Mount Fury and the Northern Pickets lie within North Cascades National Park proper, not the adjoining Ross Lake National Recreation Area.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: No Northwest Forest Pass is needed — the trailhead and route lie within the National Park; the backcountry permit itself is the required authorization.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone), fee per person, not free
overnight_permit.where: The Luna cross-country zone cannot be reserved; get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Hannegan-side permits can also be picked up at the Glacier Public Service Center on its limited summer days.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (State Route 20)
road.status: Paved to the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134; closed seasonally in winter.
road.driveNote: From Marblemount, drive east on SR 20 about 28 miles to the Ross Dam trailhead pullout (milepost 134).
road.seasonalGate: SR 20 typically closes for the season in early December between Ross Dam (MP 134) and the Silver Star gate (MP 171) and reopens in April or May depending on snowpack and avalanche conditions; in 2026 the opening was delayed further by storm damage and a spring rockslide.

climate.fall: Weather deteriorates quickly after early-mid September with returning snow
climate.spring: Heavy, lingering wet snowpack into June/July; high avalanche and stream-crossing hazard on approach
climate.summer: Jul-Aug is the primary climbing season with the most stable weather, though afternoon thunderstorms occur
climate.winter: Heavy wet snow, high avalanche danger, and SR-20 access closed
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with a heavy winter snowpack; the Pickets hold snow late into summer, and the route is rarely reliably snow-free before late July. August is the most common summit month, though brief, intense Cascade thunderstorms are common in late summer and this route offers no fast retreat once on the exposed connecting ridge.

bySeason.fall: By September, glacier crossings become icier and more crevassed, and weather windows shorten significantly.
bySeason.summer: Late July-August is prime season, offering the best balance of consolidated snow on the East Mount Fury Glacier and stable rock; watch for afternoon thunderstorm buildup.

climate.forecastZone: No dedicated NWAC avalanche forecast zone covers this cross-country summer climbing objective; check NOAA point forecasts for the Ross Lake/North Cascades backcountry before committing to the traverse.

emergency.notes: This is one of the most remote climbing objectives in Washington — multi-day evacuation time should be expected for any incident. Carry a satellite communicator (e.g., inReach) and leave a detailed trip plan with a firm return date; call 911 for search-and-rescue coordination, which the NPS coordinates with county Sheriff's Offices.

emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Dr, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284 — (360) 856-6021, open 24 hours
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Whatcom County Sheriff's Office (dispatch via 911); Whatcom County Search & Rescue / Bellingham Mountain Rescue respond to North Cascades incidents

crowds.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed; if attempted at all, almost always in July-August as part of a broader Northern Pickets traverse rather than a standalone objective
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Well under 10 parties/summits per season - as of 2016 fewer than 20 parties total had ever reached the West Fury summit

fitnessSpec.hiking: Must sustain 10-16+ hour days of bushwhacking, glacier travel, and scrambling on consecutive days with a loaded pack; the East-to-West Fury traverse alone typically takes 2.5+ hours one-way on top of an already long day
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Multi-day expedition load (glacier/crevasse rescue gear, technical rack, bivy gear, several days of food) - expect 40+ lb packs

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day approach (commonly 3-5+ days round trip as part of a Northern Pickets traverse); reaching West Fury adds roughly two and a half hours of loose ridge each way beyond the East Fury summit, turning the summit day into a 12-16 hour effort (with possible forced bivouac)
requiredSkills: low 5th class rock scrambling with exposure
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Expedition-level alpine climber with multi-day glacier travel and Grade III-IV alpine rock experience; this is not a route for anyone without prior North Cascades or comparably remote alpine terrain

July.reason: Early-to-mid July can still have significant snow cover on approach and glacier; conditions improve through the month as the season's best window opens

June.reason: Route and approach typically still snowbound and dangerous; high avalanche/wet-snow hazard and difficult stream crossings

August.reason: Core of the best-season window; most stable glacier and rock conditions, lowest crevasse-bridge risk, best weather odds

September.reason: Early September remains within the established best-season window, but early-fall storms and shortening daylight increase risk on this multi-day objective

weather.typical: Severe, remote alpine environment; short reliable summer window with colder, storm-prone conditions bracketing it in fall and essentially unattempted conditions in winter
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving weather systems are a real risk in the North Cascades in summer; multi-day exposure on this traverse means parties are very likely to encounter at least one weather event during a typical trip

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence - the exposed traverse between the East and West summits combines loose rock with sustained exposure on a long, convoluted low-5th-class ridge; a slip or rockfall incident this deep in the Pickets carries an extremely long, difficult self-rescue or evacuation

avalanche.zone: N/A - no NWAC forecast zone specifically covers this remote North Cascades National Park objective; nearest general guidance would be the NWAC Cascade Pass/Eldorado area forecasts, but this is not a wintertime objective

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Significant hazard - changing crevasse conditions on the northwest flank glacier approach and the exposed east-west summit traverse; parties describe snow-bridge crossings between roughly 7,400-7,800 ft and crevasses requiring jumps during descent, so risk is real and route-finding-dependent through the season

gaps: First ascent details specific to West Peak itself (as opposed to East Peak) are not well documented in available sources; the 1938 Ptarmigan Climbing Club date on file is the date traditionally associated with the first ascent of Mount Fury generally, and a summit register reportedly bearing that party's names has been found on the West Peak summit, but this could not be independently confirmed as the true FA of the harder West summit specifically.

The exact col elevation between East and West Fury (the basis for West Peak's listed 358 ft prominence) was not independently re-verified in this research pass, though it is broadly consistent with described saddle terrain in trip reports.

No guidebook-grade pitch-by-pitch topo exists for the East-to-West Fury connecting ridge; the description here is compiled from multiple trip reports (Mountain Project, personal blogs) rather than a single authoritative source.
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Newhalem, drive SR-20 east about 14 miles; the trailhead parking is on the right between mileposts 134 and 135.

before.corrections: The peak's elevationFt is currently null in the database; the best current figure for West Fury's summit is ~8,305 ft ±10 ft per Eric Gilbertson's October 2022 theodolite survey (older USGS-quad-derived figures cite 8,292-8,298 ft). No specific first-ascent record for this connecting-ridge/scramble line (as distinct from the peak's original ascent) could be sourced, so 'fa' is left null rather than guessed.
before.rappel_count_note: Parties make one or two single-rope-length rappels where they choose to, over the 4th-class and low-5th-class steps along the ridge; where these fall is not published, so no stations are listed.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek to Access Col, then the sidehill traverse around Luna Peak to the Fury-Luna connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at milepost 134, this is a multi-day approach and not a day hike. The standard option follows the Big Beaver Trail: hike, or take the seasonal water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, roughly 6 miles up the west shore of Ross Lake to the Big Beaver Creek trailhead, then the maintained trail up-valley through old-growth cedar past the Big Beaver and Luna camps to a point about 1.5 miles north of Luna Camp, roughly 10-11 trail miles in.

Leave the trail there, ford Big Beaver Creek and climb steep pathless forest and heather along the north side of Access Creek to break out into the open, meadow-floored Access Creek basin below Luna Peak, which is relatively brush-free compared with neighbouring drainages. Continue up-basin past a camping area near the headwaters, then climb a steep gully and heather system to a notch around 6,100 ft, Access Col, which gives the first view north into Luna Cirque and the Southern Pickets skyline.

From the col a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass and Luna Cirque, then gains the Fury-Luna connecting ridge.
hazards: Picking the wrong drainage off the Big Beaver Trail in poor visibility, a documented error here
Cliff-band route-finding on broken ledges where a wrong tier cliffs you out
Poor, vegetated rock that takes gear badly, and shockingly mobile large talus on the summit ridges of the massif
Gullies dropping into Access Creek involve cliffy downclimbing and occasionally short rappels
Water is abundant along Big Beaver and Access Creeks but scarce above Access Col
One of the most remote summits in the range, with no quick way off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route is entered from a small glacier, not from a ridge, and that is the discriminator. The northwest side of West Fury is reached by a small glacier tucked beneath the peak, gained from the ridge system running toward Luna. Snow travel on it is reported as straightforward and kickable in good conditions. If you are scrambling rock to reach the start of this route you are in the wrong place; the start is where you step off snow onto dirty, ledge-broken ground on the northwest flank.

The route-finding warning is the base finding, because the mistake happens here: leaving the glacier, you work up broken ledge bands to gain the west ridge crest. The rock is poor and vegetated with few obvious anchors, and A wrong tier will cliff you out. Route-finding through the ledge bands is the real difficulty, not the climbing. Pick the tier that keeps going; if you have to make a hard move to stay on a ledge, you are on the wrong one.

Confirm higher: from the crest, an ascending traverse east across loose rock leads into a chute that tops out slightly east of the summit. Topping out east of the top and having to walk back west is correct on this line, not an error.

What does not belong here: this line is documented mainly as a descent by parties traversing the Northern Pickets rather than as a commonly repeated ascent. Expect to be route-finding from first principles and treat any confident-sounding description of the ledges, including this one, as less precise than it sounds.

A named navigation hazard lower down, which is where the day is actually lost: poor visibility has caused parties to pick the wrong drainage off the Big Beaver Trail. Some parties cairn the correct creek crossing on the way in. Access Creek's basin is the open, meadow-floored, relatively brush-free one; if you are fighting continuous brush you are in a neighbouring drainage.

climbing_route.label: Small glacier northwest of the peak
climbing_route.notes: The northwest side is reached by a small glacier tucked beneath the peak, gained from the ridge system running toward Luna. Snow travel here is reported as straightforward and kickable in good conditions, but it is glacier terrain and the surrounding ground is broken. Note that this line is documented mainly as a descent by parties traversing the Northern Pickets rather than as a commonly repeated ascent, so expect to be route-finding from first principles.

climbing_route.label: Ledges to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: Leave the glacier and work up dirty, ledge-broken terrain on the northwest flank to gain the west ridge crest. The rock is poor and vegetated, with few obvious anchors; parties descending this ground have found it slow and awkward rather than technically hard. Route-finding through the ledge bands is the real difficulty and a wrong tier can cliff you out.

climbing_route.label: Ascending traverse and summit chute
climbing_route.notes: From the crest, an ascending traverse east across loose rock leads into a chute that tops out slightly east of the summit. Everything on this upper section is described as choss, including shockingly mobile large talus on the summit ridges of the massif generally. Retreat is the concern that dominates: this is one of the most remote summits in the range, the rock takes gear poorly, and there is no quick way off.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

before.overview: Little Annapurna (8,485 ft) is a granite summit in the Core (Upper) Enchantments, Stuart Range, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, immediately south of the Enchantment Lakes basin near Isolation and Tranquil Lakes. It was named by Ellensburg's Sherpa Climbing Club for its resemblance to the Himalayan Annapurna massif. The North Slopes route is the easiest way up the peak, an enjoyable Class 2-3 scramble typically approached via Aasgard Pass, finishing with a short 3rd-class step onto the small summit pedestal and views of Dragontail Peak, the Knitting/Nightmare Needles, and the Enchantment Lakes.
before.beta: From the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trailhead, hike to Colchuck Lake and grind up the steep boulder-and-scree gully of Aasgard Pass to reach the upper Enchantment basin. From the pass, head roughly south-southwest past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes toward Little Annapurna's northeast ridge, then follow cairns up open granite slabs and talus on the peak's north side to the summit -- one of three rocky high points on the ridge, with the true summit being the middle one. The line itself involves minimal exposure and only occasional Class 3 moves, but Aasgard Pass is the physical and route-finding crux of the day.
before.turnaround: The route is short, so weather is the deciding factor. Be off the open summit plateau before afternoon storms, which can build quickly over the Enchantments.
before.face: Standard route: upper Enchantments basin and the peak's north/west-facing slopes, ascending near (west of) the northeast ridge
before.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
before.comms: Parties report no cell service at the trailhead or anywhere along the approach and route; a satellite communicator (e.g., inReach) is recommended for emergencies.
before.descent: Reverse the NE-flank scramble to the plateau, then retrace the route back over Aasgard Pass and down to Colchuck Lake and the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail. Early season the Aasgard Pass headwall can often be glissaded; by late summer it is loose talus/scree, and the descent is typically slower and harder on the knees than the climb up.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive Eightmile Road (FR-7601) to its end at the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake trailhead, about 3,500 ft. Overnight stays in the Colchuck Zone need a quota wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail #1599 about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599.1 splits left and south. Continue roughly 1.8 miles more, crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet, to the lake at 5,570 ft. This is the last easy, reliable water, so fill here because there is none above.

waypoints.name: Aasgard Pass
waypoints.directions: Skirt the lake's south and east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the foot of the obvious steep gully and headwall at the head of the lake. Aasgard gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping; cairns get knocked over and the path splits into several use trails, so keep re-picking the line toward the notch. Firm snow and ice can linger into July, making an axe and sometimes crampons worthwhile on what is otherwise a scramble.

waypoints.name: Core Enchantments
waypoints.directions: From the pass, cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core Zone past Tranquil Lake (Lake Freya) and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

waypoints.name: Base of north slopes
waypoints.directions: Near the far end of the meadows, watch for an unsigned climbers' path forking right, to the west, toward Little Annapurna. If you cross a stream and pass a toilet sign you have gone by the junction and should backtrack.

waypoints.name: Little Annapurna summit
waypoints.directions: Above here it is a scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths rather than a trail. Take the line of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east side, switchbacking and scrambling at low 3rd class at most. The true summit is the middle of three rocky high points along the crest.

before.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed.
pro_tips: Combine it with nearby Core summits in one outing.

before.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing; movement is unroped scrambling. The challenge is minimal beyond basic route-finding and staying back from the south edge.
before.best_season: Late June/July through early October for a snow-free scramble; the Aasgard Pass headwall and upper slopes often hold snow well into July, so an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is recommended early season. Late September brings the Enchantment basin's famous larch color along with its heaviest crowds and permit competition.
before.approach: From the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of Eightmile Road/FR-7601), follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) splits left/south. Continue roughly 1.8 more miles — crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet — to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3 mi in), the last easy, reliable water before the pass. Skirt the lake's south/east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the base of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep gully/headwall at the lake's south end. Aasgard Pass is the crux of the approach: it gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on a mix of dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping, cairns are frequently knocked down and the path braids into several use-trails, and well into summer it can still hold firm snow/ice that makes an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) worthwhile even though the route is otherwise a scramble. Top out at Aasgard Pass (~7,800-7,841 ft, ~5.3 mi from the trailhead). Beyond the pass, cross the grey talus/glacial-till 'moonscape' of the upper Core Zone past Tranquil Lake (Lake Freya) and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets. Near the far end of these meadows watch for an unsigned climbers' path forking right (west) toward Little Annapurna — crossing a stream and passing a toilet sign means you've overshot the junction. From there the route is more a scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths than a trail; pick the path of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling (low 3rd class at most) to the 8,485-ft summit. Trailhead-to-summit totals run about 15-16 miles and 5,000-5,800 ft. Hazards: no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet, so fill up there; loose rock and rockfall potential on Aasgard Pass and the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun/thunderstorm exposure on the open talus above the pass; and early/mid-season snow on the pass creating slip-and-slide fall hazard.
before.descent_text: Reverse the North Slopes: downclimb the low-3rd-class/class-2 slabs and talus on the peak's east side back to the col/basin, pick up the braided boot paths back through the Brisingamen Lakelets meadows, and rejoin the Core Zone trail past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes to Aasgard Pass. This is a scramble walk-off in both directions — no rope, rack, or rappelling is used on the standard North Slopes line; parties simply describe reversing the ascent, and the peak is often characterized as little more than a steep class 2 hike. The one genuine descent-specific hazard is Aasgard Pass itself: down-climbing its ~2,000 ft of loose scree and talus in the afternoon (often with the sun having softened any remaining snow, and other parties ascending below) is a common cause of rockfall incidents and slips — down-climb deliberately, stay out of others' fall line, and only glissade if a real, clean snow chute with a safe runout is in (by mid-to-late summer the pass is usually bare, exposed talus rather than snow). From the base of the pass, retrace the trail around Colchuck Lake and down the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead. Rappels: 0.
before.bail: Retreat is trivial by reversing the scramble at any point, with no committing terrain. The only real caution is keeping well back from the abrupt south edge of the summit plateau.

pitch_detail.notes: Ascend granite slabs and blocks on the peak's north side/slopes to the summit, following cairns; occasional Class 3 moves are possible depending on the exact line chosen. The true summit is the middle of three rocky high points.

itinerary.cal: Camping at Colchuck Lake requires a quota Colchuck Zone wilderness permit (lottery in winter, limited walk-up availability) for the roughly late-May–Oct season; Aasgard Pass often still holds snow/ice into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season trips.

days.note: Hike from the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead via the Colchuck Lake Trail (moderate, well-graded climb through forest and boulder fields) to camp at Colchuck Lake, 5,570 ft. Most parties use this shorter approach day to bank energy and scout the Aasgard Pass gully before the long summit day.

days.note: An early alpine start up the steep, loose Aasgard Pass gully (2,200+ ft in under 2 miles) gains the Enchantment plateau, from which an easy walk-up leads to the summit. Most parties then descend the full route back through camp, break down their tent, and continue all the way out to the trailhead the same day — a long, full day, so an early start matters and headlamps for the final miles are common.

Strong, fit parties do sometimes push it car-to-car in a single very long day (~12-13 hrs), but most treat it as an overnight given the permit system and the risk of descending the loose Aasgard Pass gully in the dark.

access.fees: $6 non-refundable lottery application fee; overnight camping fee of $5 per person per night (May 15-October 31); a Northwest Forest Pass is required for trailhead parking at the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead.
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft and within 0.5 mile of any lake, which effectively bans fires along the entire approach and on the peak; dogs are prohibited throughout the Enchantment Permit Area; group size is capped at 8 in the Colchuck/Stuart zones; camp only at established sites on rock, gravel, or sand.
access.permit: Overnight camping anywhere in the Enchantment Permit Area (including the Colchuck and Stuart zones used to approach Little Annapurna, and the Core Zone around Isolation/Tranquil Lakes) requires a permit via Recreation.gov, allocated mostly through the advance lottery held mid-February to March 1 (results posted mid-March), with a limited number of rolling 7-day-window/walk-up releases through the rest of the season.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (lottery, not free) May 15 to Oct 31; self-issue at the trailhead the rest of the year
overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

crowds.peakTraffic: Late-September larch season and July-August weekends, when the Core Enchantments zone is at its busiest with permit holders and thru-hikers; Little Annapurna itself sees noticeably less traffic than the main lake basin since it is an optional side-scramble rather than the thru-hike route
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Core Enchantments permit holders number in the hundreds per season (one of the most competitive lotteries in WA), but likely only a few dozen parties actually detour to summit Little Annapurna specifically

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong — able to sustain 15+ mile, 5,000-6,000 ft days if day-tripping the whole loop, or carry overnight gear over Aasgard Pass to a Core camp and do the summit as a shorter 4-hr round trip from there
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight pack (roughly 30-40 lb) if camping in the Core zone; fast-and-light day pack only for parties attempting it as a single huge push

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long — the peak is reached from a Core Enchantments camp (the top of Aasgard Pass, where the Core begins, is roughly 6 mi and ~4,400 ft of gain from the Stuart Lake trailhead); the summit push from camp is about 4 hrs round trip
requiredSkills: Class 2-3 scrambling on loose talus and slabs
off-trail routefinding across similar-looking granite terrain in the basin
steep, loose, unmaintained trail/scree competence for the Aasgard Pass approach
early-season snow travel and basic self-arrest if attempting before full melt-out
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable with sustained Class 2-3 off-trail scrambling and long alpine days; should already have Enchantments-caliber backcountry experience given the approach

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through October, with late September the standout window for larch color and stable weather

July.reason: Early month can still hold lingering snowfields on north-facing terrain and on the Aasgard Pass approach; conditions firm up through the month

August.reason: Driest, most stable month with slabs and talus mostly clear of snow

October.reason: Shorter days and possible early snow/freezing temps as the season closes out; larches have dropped needles

September.reason: Stable fall weather and famous larch color late in the month though this is also the most crowded stretch

weather.typical: A short summer-to-fall scramble best done July through October, with late September larch season especially scenic
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a known risk on the exposed summit plateau — check forecasts and turn around early if storms are building

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate — Class 2-3 talus/slab terrain; an abrupt drop-off on the south side of the summit plateau, so straying off-route in poor visibility or storm is the main fall hazard, compounded by loose underfoot rock throughout

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble climbed July-Oct, outside NWAC's typical Nov-Apr forecast season

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of Eightmile Road/FR-7601)

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's left of the cliff bands. Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain climber's right near the waterfalls, with fatalities on record
Misleading and duplicated cairns on the pass and on the peak itself
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above, on the pass and on the final slopes
No water past the Colchuck Lake outlet
Full sun and thunderstorm exposure on open talus above the pass — no shelter anywhere in the Core
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two separate 'find it' problems on this route and the first one is the trail junction, not the mountain.

Near the far end of the meadows, watch for an unsigned path forking right (west) toward Little Annapurna. It is a use-path, not tread. The unambiguous overshoot marker is downstream of it: if you cross a small stream and pass a sign for the toilet, you have gone too far and need to come back. That pair — stream then toilet sign — is the single most useful navigational fact on this route, because the junction itself has nothing to see.

From the pass at Aasgard, Little Annapurna lies to the southeast and reads as a gently rolling hill rather than a peak, which is part of why people walk past the turn.

The second problem is the mountain itself, and the honest answer is that there is no single line. The 'route' is a scatter of well-worn boot paths over broad north-facing slabs and talus. Cairns are present, easy to lose, and mark more than one option. The working rule reported by everyone: take the path of least resistance up the peak's left (east) side, switchbacking and scrambling, nothing harder than low 3rd class, to the summit at 8,485 ft.

If you find yourself on anything that feels like real climbing, you have drifted off the line — this is a walk-up with hands occasionally on rock, and any steepening means come back left and lower.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
approach_variants.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.
approach_variants.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges on the pass
Punchy afternoon snow over hidden ice
Patchy snow-to-slab transitions on the summit slopes
Uncontrolled glissade descending the pass — the classic afternoon incident here
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Early summer and the shoulder seasons, when the pass still holds snow; same line, but bring an ice axe and crampons and take care descending the softened snow in the afternoon.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow covering the Core, the unsigned right-hand fork toward Little Annapurna and the stream-then-toilet-sign overshoot marker are all buried or unreliable, so navigate by the lakes instead: from the top of Aasgard, travel between Isolation Lake and Tranquil Lake and then head south toward the broad rolling summit mass that sits southeast of the pass.

On the peak, snow simplifies the problem — the braided boot paths and contradictory cairns that make the summer scramble confusing are gone, and the broad north-facing slopes go directly. Keep to the left (east) side of the mountain and take the easiest angle available.

What to watch for instead: the transition from snow to bare slab, which happens patchily on a north-facing slope in early summer and is where an unroped slip becomes a slide.

climbing_route.label: North slabs and talus to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths rather than a trail: pick the path of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling to the 8,485-ft summit. Loose rock and rockfall potential on the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun and thunderstorm exposure on the open talus; no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

road.name: Mowich Lake Road
road.status: No public vehicle, bike or foot access via SR 165: the Fairfax Bridge over the Carbon River has been permanently closed since April 2025, with no detour and no date to reopen.
road.driveNote: Mowich Lake is now reached only on foot, a walk in of roughly 20 to 30 miles depending on the start (Westside Road, Sunrise, Longmire, or up the Carbon River). Plan this climb as a backpacking trip and carry the park’s overnight wilderness permit.

set.approach: Mowich Lake is no longer a drive-up trailhead (see the road note): reaching it is a long walk in of its own. From the Mowich Lake trailhead, take the Spray Park Trail (the Wonderland Trail at first) about 3.5 miles to Spray Park at roughly 5,800 ft. Near 6,200 ft a way trail leaves the main trail, easy to follow for about a mile, and climbs toward the saddle between Echo Rock and Observation Rock near 7,600 ft. Stay on snow where you can to spare the meadows. The north side of Observation is steep and loose, so contour clockwise round the foot of the peak, crossing the east icefield of the Flett Glacier if it is in, to the scree and talus of the south slope, where the climb starts.

before.name: Standard scramble route
pro_tips: Going from Echo's base to Observation, descend to the glacier and use the boot path rather than side-hilling loose scree.
Many August parties go over Knapsack Pass (about an hour from the lake) and drop to the Spray Park trail, returning by the trail.
Budget about 12 to 13 miles round trip and roughly 3,800 to 4,200 ft of gain.
Early August brings mosquitoes at the lake and through Spray Park; carry repellent.
watch_out: Rockfall peels off Echo Rock onto the east side of the Flett in August
Scree beside the glacier can sit on bare ice in late September; stay on the glacier surface instead

Near 6,200 ft a way trail leaves the main trail, easy to follow for about a mile, and climbs toward the saddle between Echo Rock and Observation Rock near 7,600 ft. Stay on snow where you can to spare the meadows. The north side of Observation is steep and loose, so contour clockwise round the foot of the peak, crossing the east icefield of the Flett Glacier if it is in, to the scree and talus of the south slope, where the climb starts.
before.descent_text: Reverse the route: down the loose pumice of the south slope to the Echo-Observation saddle, then back along the way trail to Spray Park and the Spray Park Trail to Mowich Lake. Descend south and east only. Dropping west puts you on the crevassed Flett Glacier, which may be impassable late in the season. By August the snow slopes east of the summit can be icy, so carry an ice axe and crampons or microspikes, or circle well above or below them. Wear a helmet, since the rock is crumbly and anything knocked loose falls on those below.

August.reason: By August the Flett Glacier is mostly bare ice with snow left only along its edges; microspikes and an axe handled it for most parties.

September.reason: By late September and early October the glacier is hard blue ice with step-over crevasses and meltwater channels, so aluminum crampons are the safer choice than spikes.
